title: Zechariah 8:1–17
context: The LORD of Armies declares his jealous love for Zion and promises to return and dwell in Jerusalem, which will be called the City of Truth. Old men and women will sit in the streets and children will play there; he will gather his people from east and west, and “They will be my people, and I will be their God.” The people are urged to let their hands be strong as the temple is rebuilt, for God will now do good to Jerusalem as surely as he once brought judgment. The section closes with ethical commands: speak truth, judge with truth and peace, and devise no evil against a neighbor. Shared ground: both traditions read these promises as God’s gracious restoration joined to a call to faithful living.

verses.text: The word of the LORD of Armies came to me.
verses.arminianNotes:
The word of the LORD of Armies comes to Zechariah. A series of promises begins.

Arminian readers see God moving from warning to hope, inviting the community to trust and obey in light of what he will do.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chapter 8 contains a series of short sayings, each introduced by “The LORD of Armies says.”

Reformed readers see God’s gracious purposes declared. Shared ground: both traditions read this as the turn from judgment in chapter 7 to restoration in chapter 8.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath.” God’s jealousy is protective.

Arminian readers see God’s passionate commitment to his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The wording closely recalls 1:14. The wrath here seems directed against Zion’s enemies, though readers differ.

Reformed readers see God’s covenant love. Shared ground: both traditions read God’s jealousy as fierce devotion, not petty envy.

verses.text: The LORD says: “I have returned to Zion, and will dwell in the middle of Jerusalem. Jerusalem shall be called ‘The City of Truth;’ and the mountain of the LORD of Armies, ‘The Holy Mountain.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he has returned to Zion and will dwell in Jerusalem, called “The City of Truth” and “The Holy Mountain.” God’s presence transforms the city.

Arminian readers see restoration grounded in God’s dwelling.
verses.reformedNotes:
Some readers hear in the return of God’s presence an answer to the departure of his glory in Ezekiel 10–11.

Reformed readers see God’s presence making the city holy. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s promise to dwell with his people.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “Old men and old women will again dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, every man with his staff in his hand because of their old age.
verses.arminianNotes:
Old men and old women will again dwell in Jerusalem’s streets, each with a staff because of age. Long life returns.

Arminian readers see peace and security restored.
verses.reformedNotes:
The picture of the elderly suggests safety after war and exile.

Reformed readers see God’s blessing on ordinary life. Shared ground: both traditions read this tender image as a sign of restored peace and stability under God’s care.

verses.text: The streets of the city will be full of boys and girls playing in its streets.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The streets will be full of boys and girls playing. Children fill the city.

Arminian readers see joy and hope returning to a community that had known desolation and loss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Together with verse 4, the image spans generations, from the oldest to the youngest.

Reformed readers see God’s blessing extending to every generation. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a warm picture of restored community life, safe for the old and the young alike.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my eyes?” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks, if this seems marvelous to the remnant, should it also be marvelous to him? Nothing is too hard for God.

Arminian readers see faith encouraged.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question addresses the remnant’s difficulty believing the promise.

Reformed readers see God’s power exceeding human expectation. Shared ground: both traditions read this as encouragement that God can do what seems impossible to a small and struggling community.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “Behold, I will save my people from the east country and from the west country.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he will save his people from the east country and the west country. The gathering is wide.

Arminian readers see God reaching his scattered people wherever they are.
verses.reformedNotes:
East and west together suggest every direction, not only Babylon.

Reformed readers see God’s saving power. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s promise to gather his people from wherever they have been scattered, a promise readers apply in different ways.

verses.text: I will bring them, and they will dwell within Jerusalem. They will be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He will bring them to dwell in Jerusalem: “They will be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.” The covenant formula returns.

Arminian readers see covenant renewal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Compare Exodus 6:7, Jeremiah 7:23, and Jeremiah 30:22, each in its own setting.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness renewed. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God renewing his covenant relationship.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “Let your hands be strong, you who hear in these days these words from the mouth of the prophets who were in the day that the foundation of the house of the LORD of Armies was laid, even the temple, that it might be built.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Let your hands be strong,” to those hearing the prophets who spoke when the temple’s foundation was laid. Encouragement to work.

Arminian readers see the call to persevere in rebuilding.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prophets in view likely include Haggai and Zechariah (compare Ezra 5:1).

Reformed readers see God strengthening his people for their task. Shared ground: both traditions read this as encouragement to faithful work.

verses.text: For before those days there was no wages for man nor any wages for an animal, neither was there any peace to him who went out or came in, because of the adversary. For I set all men everyone against his neighbor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Before those days there were no wages for man or animal, and no peace for those going out or coming in, because of the adversary; God set people against each other. Hard times are recalled.

Arminian readers see judgment in the past.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse looks back to the hardship before the rebuilding began (compare Haggai 1).

Reformed readers see God’s hand in hardship. Shared ground: both traditions read this as remembrance of discipline.

verses.text: But now I will not be to the remnant of this people as in the former days,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
But now the LORD will not treat the remnant as in the former days. A new season begins.

Arminian readers see God’s favor restored to those who have returned to rebuild.
verses.reformedNotes:
The contrast between “former days” and “now” is the hinge of the chapter.

Reformed readers see God’s mercy following judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s gracious change toward the remnant, opening a time of blessing after years of hardship.

verses.text: “For the seed of peace and the vine will yield its fruit, and the ground will give its increase, and the heavens will give their dew. I will cause the remnant of this people to inherit all these things.
verses.arminianNotes:
The seed of peace, the vine, the ground, and the heavens will yield their fruit, and the remnant will inherit all these things. Creation blesses.

Arminian readers see covenant blessing restored.
verses.reformedNotes:
The images echo covenant blessings of fruitful land and rain.

Reformed readers see God’s generosity to his people. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s promise of material and communal blessing for the returned remnant.

verses.text: It shall come to pass that, as you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you shall be a blessing. Don’t be afraid. Let your hands be strong.”
verses.arminianNotes:
As they were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so God will save them and they will be a blessing. “Don’t be afraid. Let your hands be strong.”

Arminian readers see reversal.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise recalls God’s purpose that his people be a blessing.

Reformed readers see God’s saving purpose. Shared ground: both traditions read this as the reversal of disgrace into blessing.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies says: “As I thought to do evil to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath,” says the LORD of Armies, “and I didn’t repent,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that as he thought to do evil to them when their fathers provoked him, “and I didn’t repent,” a comparison follows. Past judgment is recalled.

Arminian readers see judgment answering provocation.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Evil” here means disaster or judgment, not moral wrong.

Reformed readers see God’s steadfast purpose in judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read this as preparing for the promise of verse 15, without opening a new divide here.

verses.text: so again I have thought in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. Don’t be afraid.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So again I have thought in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. Don’t be afraid.” God’s purpose is now good.

Arminian readers see God’s favor toward a responsive people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse matches verse 14: as God’s judgment was firm, so is his purpose of blessing.

Reformed readers see God’s gracious resolve. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s firm intention to do good to his people.

verses.text: These are the things that you shall do: speak every man the truth with his neighbor. Execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates,
verses.arminianNotes:
These are the things they shall do: speak truth with one’s neighbor and execute “the judgment of truth and peace” in the gates. Ethics follow promise.

Arminian readers see grateful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The gates were where legal disputes were settled.

Reformed readers see renewed people walking in God’s ways. Shared ground: both traditions read this as the moral shape of restored life.

verses.text: and let none of you devise evil in your hearts against his neighbor, and love no false oath; for all these are things that I hate,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let none devise evil in their hearts against a neighbor, or love a false oath, “for all these are things that I hate,” says the LORD. God names what he hates.

Arminian readers see heart and speech under God’s claim.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse echoes 7:10, now within a promise of restoration.

Reformed readers see God’s holiness shaping his people. Shared ground: both traditions read this as clear teaching on honesty and goodwill.
